lead: The PIC16F877A is an 8-bit microcontroller from the mid-range PIC family. It keeps program and data in separate memories (Harvard), uses 14-bit instruction words and offers only 35 instructions. The address field inside an instruction is only 7 bits, so it can name 128 locations out of the 368-byte data RAM; RP1:RP0 in STATUS supply the missing high bits and split the RAM into four banks. A two-stage pipeline fetches the next instruction while the present one executes. You find such chips in energy meters, battery chargers, washing machines and small card readers, where a cheap part must read sensors, count pulses and switch outputs.
prereq: You need: Chapter 2.1 and the Harvard and RISC ideas from Unit 1.

sections.h3: Data path, instruction word and pipeline

blocks.text: The core is 8 bits wide. All arithmetic and logic happens in the ALU, which takes one operand from the working register W and the other from a file register in data memory, or, for the literal instructions (MOVLW, ADDLW, ANDLW, IORLW, XORLW, SUBLW, RETLW), from the 8-bit operand field inside the 14-bit instruction word. The result goes back to W or to the file register, and the destination bit of the instruction chooses which.

Harvard separation matters here. Program memory has its own 14-bit bus and data memory has an 8-bit bus, so an instruction fetch and a data read can happen together, and code can never be overwritten by a stray pointer. Every instruction is exactly one 14-bit word: a 6-bit opcode plus up to 8 bits of operand. The whole instruction set is 35 instructions.

The pipeline has two stages. While an instruction executes, the next one is fetched. That is why an instruction takes one instruction cycle, written T<sub>cy</sub>, where T<sub>cy</sub> = 4 × T<sub>OSC</sub>. A 4 MHz crystal gives T<sub>OSC</sub> = 0.25 µs and T<sub>cy</sub> = 1 µs. When a jump or call is taken, the word already fetched is wrong, so it is discarded and the pipeline refills: that instruction costs 2 T<sub>cy</sub>.

sections.h3: Program memory, banks and the hardware stack

blocks.text: Program memory is 8K × 14 flash: 8192 words of 14 bits, addressed from 0000H to 1FFFH. Two addresses are fixed by hardware. After reset the CPU starts at 0000H; an interrupt sends it to 0004H. Put a jump at 0000H, and your interrupt routine or a jump to it at 0004H. The 8-level hardware stack stores return addresses only; it is not for data.

Data memory is 368 bytes of RAM, plus 256 bytes of EEPROM for values that must survive a power cut. The RAM is split into four banks of up to 128 bytes. A direct address inside an instruction is only 7 bits, so it can name a cell within one bank but cannot say which bank. The bits RP1:RP0 in STATUS choose the bank.

items: W: the working register. It is not in data memory and has no address.
STATUS, address 03H: holds RP1, RP0, IRP, the zero flag Z, digit carry DC and carry C.
FSR, 04H: an 8-bit pointer used for indirect addressing.
INDF, 00H: reading or writing INDF actually touches the cell that FSR points to.
PCL, 02H, and PCLATH, 0AH: PCL is the low 8 bits of the program counter; PCLATH holds the upper bits and must be written before a computed jump.

blocks.text: Indirect addressing ignores RP1:RP0. FSR supplies the low 7 bits and its bit 7 picks one bank of a pair, while IRP (bit 7 of STATUS) picks the pair: IRP = 0 means banks 0 and 1, IRP = 1 means banks 2 and 3. So FSR = A0H with IRP = 1 reaches physical address 1A0H in bank 3.
The 16F877A is a 40-pin part. Around the core sit the blocks that make it a microcontroller rather than a CPU.

items: Timer0 (8-bit), Timer1 (16-bit) and Timer2 (8-bit) for timing and counting pulses.
CCP modules: capture an edge, compare against a value, or generate PWM.
MSSP: a synchronous serial port for SPI and I2C.
USART: asynchronous serial, for a PC link or a radio module.
A 10-bit ADC with 8 input channels, so an analog sensor reads as a number from 0 to 1023.
Ports A to E, 33 I/O pins in total, each pin's direction set by a TRIS register.

blocks.text: Timers, interrupts, PWM and the ADC are detailed in Unit 3; SPI, I2C and UART frames are in Unit 4. Here you only need this: these blocks hang off the same 8-bit data bus and appear as file registers in banks 0 and 1.

sections.h3: Changing banks in a real program

blocks.text: Bank switching is the step where marks are lost, so do it in a fixed order. Instruction syntax is covered in Chapter 2.6.

items: Decide the target bank and the 7-bit address of the register inside it.
Set or clear RP1:RP0 in STATUS, for example BSF STATUS,RP0 to reach bank 1.
Access the register by its 7-bit address; hardware adds the bank bits for you.
Repeat for every other bank you touch. The RP bits stay where you left them.
Restore the original RP1:RP0 before returning, if the calling code expects that bank.

blocks.text: Two common bugs. A subroutine changes RP0 and returns without restoring it, so the caller's next write lands in the wrong bank. Or PCLATH is not updated before a computed jump, and the jump lands on the wrong 2K page.

figure.caption: The 8-bit ALU and W sit between a 14-bit program memory and banked data memory. STATUS (address 03H) holds the value 21H, i.e. RP0 = 1, and points direct accesses at data bank 1, while FSR and INDF reach the same memory as a pointer.

spec.title: PIC16F877A core and memory
spec.aria: PIC16F877A fetches 14-bit instructions from 8K×14 program memory through a two-stage pipeline, and STATUS value 21H (address 03H) selects data bank 1.

examples.question: A program on a PIC16F877A writes the value 21H into the STATUS register. (a) Which data-memory bank is selected for direct addressing? (b) Which bits of RP1:RP0 are set, and which arithmetic flag is set? (c) Give 21H in decimal.
steps: The STATUS bit order is IRP(7), RP1(6), RP0(5), TO(4), PD(3), Z(2), DC(1), C(0).

Read the writable status bits from the written value: IRP = 0, RP1 = 0, RP0 = 1, Z = 0, DC = 0, C = 1. TO (bit 4) and PD (bit 3) are read-only; a write to STATUS does not change them. After power-up or a CLRWDT both are 1, so they keep TO = 1 and PD = 1 rather than taking 0 from 21H.
RP1:RP0 = 01, so the bank number is 0×2 + 1 = 1. Direct addresses in the instruction now refer to data bank 1.
C = 1, so the carry flag is set; Z = 0 and DC = 0.
examples.answer: RP1:RP0 = 01 selects data bank 1, the carry flag C = 1 is set, and 21H = 33 decimal.
examples.check:
status = 0x21
rp1 = (status >> 6) & 1
rp0 = (status >> 5) & 1
bank = rp1 * 2 + rp0
carry = status & 1
print(bank)
print(rp0)
print(rp1)
print(carry)
print(status)

traps: W has no address. It is not in the data memory map, so you cannot reach it with FSR or with a bank bit; only the destination bit of an instruction names it.
RP1:RP0 select the bank for direct addressing only. Indirect addressing through INDF uses IRP plus bit 7 of FSR, and ignores RP1:RP0.
14-bit is the instruction width, 8-bit is the data width. Writing that the PIC has a 14-bit data bus is a common wrong answer.
The 8-level hardware stack holds return addresses only, pushed by CALL and by an interrupt; it is not for data. Data must be pushed by hand into RAM, not into this stack.
A taken branch costs 2 T<sub>cy</sub>, not 1. The pipeline overlaps fetch with execute but does not remove the refill cost after a jump.

quiz.q: State the reset vector and the interrupt vector of the PIC16F877A.
How many instructions does the PIC16F877A have, and how wide is one instruction word?
Why does the PIC16F877A need bank-select bits at all?
quiz.a: A direct address in an instruction is only 7 bits, so it can name 1 of 128 locations. RAM has 368 bytes, so RP1:RP0 in STATUS supply the missing high bits and select one of four banks.

quiz.q: W is called a register but has no address. What does that mean for instruction operands?
quiz.a: W is not in the data memory map, so no address or pointer can reach it. Instructions name it through the destination bit (0 = W, 1 = file register), and to store W in RAM you must copy it with an instruction such as MOVWF.

quiz.q: A PIC16F877A runs from a 4 MHz crystal. Find T<sub>OSC</sub>, T<sub>cy</sub>, and the time taken by a GOTO that is taken.
quiz.a: T<sub>OSC</sub> = 1/4 MHz = 0.25 µs. T<sub>cy</sub> = 4 × 0.25 µs = 1 µs. A taken GOTO takes 2 T<sub>cy</sub> = 2 µs.

quiz.q: FSR = A0H and IRP = 1. Which bank does INDF access, and what is the physical address?
quiz.a: IRP = 1 selects the bank pair 2 and 3. Bit 7 of FSR is 1, so bank 3 is used. Physical address = 1A0H, which is offset 20H inside bank 3.

quiz.q: A subroutine sets RP0 = 1, writes one byte, and returns without clearing RP0. Explain the bug for the caller.
quiz.a: RP1:RP0 are global state, not saved by the call. After return the caller's direct address, say 20H, is decoded inside bank 1 as A0H instead of inside bank 0 as 20H, so the caller silently writes a different cell. The subroutine must restore the bank bits, or the caller must set them before every access.

quiz.q: Why does a taken branch cost two instruction cycles when a normal instruction costs one?
quiz.a: The two-stage pipeline has already fetched the next sequential instruction while the branch executes. When the branch is taken, that word is not the one needed, so it is discarded and a fresh fetch starts; execute waits one extra T<sub>cy</sub> for the refill.

beyond: Not for the exam. Later PIC families keep the same Harvard idea but widen things: PIC18 uses 16-bit instructions and an optional priority interrupt scheme, and PIC24/dsPIC use 24-bit instructions with a 16-bit data path. Microchip's newer enhanced mid-range parts add more instructions while staying close to the 16F877A, so a lab board of this device still teaches the family. Competing 8-bit cores, such as AVR and the ARM Cortex-M0+, are worth comparing on instruction width and register file. Search for the device datasheet, then for the enhanced mid-range and PIC18 programming manuals.
